items.item: the application itself owns the read-miss path under cache-aside, checking the cache first and only then querying the data store and writing the result back

at.step: Reveal: cache-aside, the application's own miss path

items.item: cache-aside's own named risk is staleness, because nothing updates the cache when the underlying data changes outside of a miss

at.step: Reveal: cache-aside, the application's own miss path

items.item: under read-through, the cache itself (not the application) delegates to the backing store on a miss, loads the value, and keeps it for next time

at.step: Reveal: read-through, the cache's own miss path

items.item: a write-through write doesn't complete until the backing store has actually been updated, which is its own named cost: no improvement to write latency at all

at.step: Reveal: write-through and write-behind, and the loss the hook already showed

items.item: write-behind returns immediately and writes the backing store asynchronously after a delay, which effectively makes the cache the system-of-record until that queue has actually been written

at.step: Hook: a write-behind cache acknowledges a write, then the node dies before the queue drains

items.item: Caffeine's own W-TinyLFU policy uses a small admission LRU gated by a TinyLFU frequency-sketch admission filter in front of a larger Segmented LRU

at.step: Reveal: LRU, LFU, and a real measured gap between them

items.item: a plain LRU cache and a frequency-gated admission policy, run against the identical skewed access pattern, measure a real, meaningfully different hit rate rather than an asserted one

at.step: Reveal: LRU, LFU, and a real measured gap between them

items.item: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-behind aren't four unrelated strategies; they're two independent choices (who owns the read miss — the application or the cache — and when a write is acknowledged — before or after the backing store lands) that happen to get four names.

at.step: Reveal: cache-aside, the application's own miss path

items.item: Moving miss-path ownership from the application to the cache (cache-aside to read-through) doesn't change the staleness risk at all — it only changes which piece of code has to know how to load from the backing store.

at.step: Reveal: read-through, the cache's own miss path

items.item: Write-behind's own loss risk isn't a bug in any particular implementation; it's the direct, unavoidable consequence of choosing to acknowledge a write before the durable store has it, the same trade write-ahead-log group commit makes deliberately and names explicitly.

at.step: Hook: a write-behind cache acknowledges a write, then the node dies before the queue drains

items.item: A TTL doesn't make cached data correct; it only puts a ceiling on how long incorrect data is allowed to keep being served before the next read is forced to ask the backing store again.

at.step: Reveal: a TTL bounds the wrong, not fixes it

items.item: Plain LRU and plain LFU both make the same mistake from opposite directions: LRU admits everything and evicts by recency alone, so a flood of one-hit-wonders can displace a key that recurs; LFU needs history before it can protect anything, so it is slow to adapt when the workload shifts. An admission filter in front of either is a defense against exactly LRU's failure mode.

at.step: Reveal: LRU, LFU, and a real measured gap between them

items.item: Swapping an eviction policy changes nothing about what gets let in to begin with; if every requested key is admitted regardless of how rarely it recurs, the cache fills with one-hit-wonders under any eviction policy, which is exactly why admission matters as much as eviction and not instead of it.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: This topic's own buffer pool parallel (introduced two topics into this chapter) is structural, not incidental: pin/unpin bookkeeping decides what can even be considered for eviction, the same role an admission filter plays here one layer up.

This topic only establishes that an eviction-plus-admission policy can keep a cache's contents useful; it says nothing about whether those contents are still correct once the underlying data changes, which is exactly the gap the next topic closes.

Write-through's own named disadvantage (missing data on a freshly spun-up, empty node) is a different failure than write-behind's loss risk, not the same one restated — write-through never loses an acknowledged write, it only has nothing cached yet for keys nobody has written since the new node appeared.
